text:
Thanks. I found Q3 quite difficult – balancing privacy with potential help felt…icky. Specifically, imagining adding data points one by one felt very cumulative; it was hard to assess each addition in isolation.

For me, the questions about fairness (Q5 and 6) are most crucial. As someone who restarted a degree, I know systemic issues can impact success. Equal recall – making sure we don’t *miss* students from any group – is vital.

I was surprised everyone seemed so willing to accept a moderate loss of accuracy for fairness (Q5.1). Perhaps others haven’t experienced feeling overlooked by systems before. Maybe an opt-out mechanism would resolve tension - letting students choose not to be included at all?

Thanks. I agree with S8 about Q3 being difficult – that cumulative effect was definitely a challenge. It’s easy to say “small improvement” to each addition, but it adds up quickly and feels intrusive. As an advisor for eleven years, I see the potential benefits, but also the risks of overreach.

For me, explainability (Q4) is paramount. If I can't understand *why* a student is flagged, I can’t effectively advise them. The high-to-moderate trade-off felt right – accuracy is important, but not at the expense of understanding. 

I’m also surprised by the widespread acceptance of losing some accuracy for fairness (Q5.1), though I appreciate the sentiment. It highlights a real tension. S8’s opt-out suggestion is excellent; giving students agency over their data would be very reassuring.

Thanks to both S8 and A2, I completely agree about Q3 – that incremental addition *did* feel unsettling. It’s a slippery slope, and it's easy to rationalise each step until you realise how much data is being used. And as someone who moved countries mid-degree, the privacy concerns felt very real for me.

I think Q4, explainability, is also key. As a student, receiving something saying “the system flagged you” without *knowing why* would feel… accusatory? It wouldn't inspire trust. 

The fairness questions were important too. I answered ‘small’ on several of the sensitive data ones because of my own experiences feeling like an outsider navigating a new system. An opt-out, as S8 suggested, is a really good idea – giving students control feels vital.

Thanks to S8, A2 and S6 for laying out those points so clearly. I agree wholeheartedly about Q3 – that incremental approach *did* feel like a creep, even though individually, some additions seem reasonable. As an advisor, I'm hyper-aware of how quickly seemingly innocuous data can paint incomplete or misleading pictures.

For me, Q4 is absolutely critical. Explainability isn’t just about trust with the student; it affects my ability to *do* my job effectively! A ‘black box’ model provides no actionable insight. 

I also strongly support S8's opt-out suggestion – that could bridge the gap on data sensitivity, and address some of the fairness concerns. We need to be transparent about how this system works, and empower students to make informed choices about their participation.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – Q3 *was* unsettling, seeing data added incrementally like that. Coming from outside the EU, privacy feels particularly important; I’m more aware of how easily data can be misused.

For me though, Q4 - explainability - is most critical. As a Masters student juggling work, receiving a flag without understanding *why* would add significant stress. It wouldn't feel like support. 

I answered 'small' to many questions about sensitive data because I value fairness, but also because my experience hasn’t necessarily been of being *overlooked*, more of struggling with adapting to a new system. The opt-out is excellent; that would alleviate my biggest concerns and build trust.

Thanks everyone, I agree with much of what’s been said – especially about Q3 feeling unsettlingly cumulative. As an advisor for three years, I see the potential value, but that incremental addition *does* feel like a privacy creep.

For me, explainability (Q4) is absolutely key. Not just for building student trust, but because I need to understand the reasoning to actually support them effectively! A vague flag isn't helpful; it needs context. 

I answered ‘moderate’ on most data additions – I think a small improvement in identifying at-risk students justifies some expansion, *with* strong safeguards. The opt-out suggestion is excellent – empowering students to control their data would be hugely reassuring and address many fairness concerns. It's also vital we have clear procedures for challenging flags.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really difficult – that incremental adding of data felt…invasive, honestly. As someone managing a chronic health condition *and* using disability support, I'm acutely aware of how easily data can be misinterpreted or used to make assumptions about my capabilities.

For me, explainability (Q4) is paramount. Receiving a flag without understanding why would be incredibly stressful given my situation – it’d feel like judgment, not help. 

I largely agree with the strong support for an opt-out; that's crucial. I also think if sensitive data *is* used, there needs to be a clear, accessible process for challenging any flags and ensuring fairness in how they're applied. It's about agency and control over my own story.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said, especially regarding Q3 – that incremental build-up *was* concerning. Coming here from overseas this year, adapting to everything has been…a process. So privacy feels particularly important to me; it's unsettling thinking about how easily data can be misinterpreted when you're already navigating a new culture and education system.

I think Q4 - explainability – is really critical too. As a first-year Masters student still getting used to things, receiving an unexplained flag would just add to the stress. I answered ‘small’ on most of the sensitive data questions because fairness matters, but having control over my data, through something like an opt-out, feels essential for building trust.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – especially about Q3 feeling unsettlingly cumulative. As someone nearing completion of my Masters after a slightly delayed pace due to my mental health condition, privacy *and* understanding feel vital. Adding data incrementally felt like a slippery slope, even if each step seemed small at first.

For me, explainability (Q4) is particularly important. Receiving an unexplained flag would be incredibly anxiety-inducing, especially knowing I’ve already been managing extra challenges. The opt-out suggestion is excellent – giving students control over their data feels essential for trust and addressing potential biases. It needs to be clear *how* decisions are made, so support can actually be tailored effectively.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said, especially about Q3 – that incremental addition of data definitely felt like it was adding up to something quite intrusive. Having dropped out once and restarted, I'm very aware of how easily systems can misinterpret things.

For me, explainability (Q4) is most important. Receiving a flag without understanding *why* would feel… defeating, honestly. It’d reinforce the feeling of being ‘behind’, not offer support. 

I answered 'small' to many questions about sensitive data because fairness is vital, but an opt-out mechanism, as suggested earlier, feels essential. Knowing I have control over my own information would make me much more comfortable with this system.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 quite difficult too – that incremental adding of data really highlighted how easily privacy can be eroded. As someone with dyslexia and receiving extra time on exams, I'm already aware of being ‘different’ within the system.

For me, explainability (Q4) is hugely important. If a model flags me, understanding *why* isn’t just about trust – it's crucial for knowing what support would actually be helpful given my learning difference. 

I answered 'small' on questions about disability data because I think it *could* improve identification if used carefully and ethically. The opt-out suggested is brilliant; it gives students like me control and reassurance that our specific needs are understood, not just reduced to a data point.

Thanks everyone. I really appreciate hearing all those perspectives – it's comforting to know others felt uneasy about Q3, that incremental addition *did* feel like a privacy creep. As someone who’s restarted a degree and lives with ADHD, the idea of being flagged without understanding *why* is genuinely scary. Explainability (Q4) feels critical - not just for trust, but because my brain works differently and I need to understand the reasoning to actually address any issues.

I strongly support the opt-out suggestion; agency over my data feels essential given my past experiences. While I answered ‘small’ on some sensitive data questions hoping it could help others, knowing *I* can choose not to participate is vital for me personally.
